t: Network ownership, movement validation, and physics
d: Learn about network ownership and its relationship to assemblies, physics, and more.
h:
The following content covers various concepts and tactics to improve security and mitigate cheating in your Roblox games. It's highly recommended that all developers read through these to ensure that your games are secure and fair for all users. Check the sidebar for additional security topics.

Network ownership is one of the more nuanced and commonly misunderstood aspects of the Roblox engine. When a player has network ownership of a part or assembly, they have complete authority over the physics simulation for those objects. By default, the server grants network ownership of unanchored parts to clients with nearby player characters to distribute the load of the physics simulation. This system improves responsiveness but creates significant security implications that every developer must understand.

Understanding network ownership

When a client has network ownership over parts (including their character), they have access to:

Assembly manipulation:

  • Teleport to any position.
  • This can be used to quickly gain ownership and control of as many unanchored parts and assemblies as the server will allow.
  • Manipulate their movement and state, such as flying or changing their speed.
  • Exploiters can set their Humanoid WalkSpeed to any value. Properties can be modified locally without firing any events on the local client, and without such property changes capable of being read from local scripts.
  • Play arbitrary animations and manipulate animation state.
  • Bypass physical obstacles and alter their collision.

Physics manipulation

  • Control the position and rotation of any unanchored parts or mechanisms, including replicating Inf or NaN components in CFrames. Set part velocities to extreme values (including Inf or NaN), which can interfere with the physics of other unanchored parts/assemblies, even those that are not owned by the exploiter. This is often used to fling other player characters and nearby parts. Manipulate the firing of Touched events, including not firing Touched at all.

Should your game necessitate gameplay-critical fully unanchored parts or assemblies, consider using the network ownership API to manually set ownership or turn off automatic ownership.

Movement validation

In competitive games, server-side validation of player movement is crucial for simulation integrity, as clients control character movement and physics. However, a universal solution doesn't exist due to varying gameplay mechanics.

Traditional methods often fall short in complex scenarios. Simple distance-over-time calculations may suffice for competitive shooters but fail in physics-intensive games involving vehicles, flight, or intricate interactions. Validation must also account for network latency.

Server authority is currently in beta and will be released soon. The most reliable solution for preventing physics and movement exploits is server authority, which moves physics simulation and movement validation entirely to the server. This eliminates the fundamental security weakness of client-controlled movement by ensuring all movement decisions are made on the server with authoritative validation.

Until server authority becomes available, developers implementing client-side validation must understand that effective approaches vary dramatically. Basic heuristics can flag innocent players with unstable connections, and straightforward speed calculations break down in games with complex movement systems. Position updates are subject to internet latency, requiring averaging over time. Many developers find that leaky bucket-style accumulators work well for handling burst movements while preventing sustained violations.

Practical implementation often requires projecting movement onto specific planes (e.g., XZ for ground-based movement) to avoid penalizing legitimate vertical movement while detecting horizontal teleportation. Games with legitimate teleportation mechanics need explicit exemption systems. Validation frequency, tolerance levels, and enforcement strategies should be tuned to each game's specific requirements.

kid.simple: To keep physics smooth, Roblox lets each player's device run the physics for their own character and for loose parts near them. That is called network ownership. It makes the game feel fast, but it also means a cheater can control those parts however they like. This page explains what cheaters can do with that power and how to think about checking player movement on the server.
kid.analogy: It is like letting each kid hold the scorecard for their own game of catch to save the referee time. It is faster, but a dishonest kid can just write whatever score they want.
keyPoints: The player who owns a part or assembly controls its physics completely.
By default, the server gives ownership of unanchored parts to players whose characters are nearby, to share the physics work.
Players always control their own character, so cheaters can teleport, fly, change their speed, play any animation, and walk through walls.
Cheaters can set owned parts to crazy values like `Inf` or `NaN`, or huge speeds, to fling other players and parts.
Cheaters can also fake Touched events, or stop them from firing.
If loose parts are important to gameplay, use the network ownership API, like `BasePart:SetNetworkOwner()`, to control who owns them.
Checking movement on the server is tricky. Simple speed checks can flag players with laggy internet, so average over time and allow for real teleports in your game.
Server authority, which runs movement on the server, is coming and is the most reliable fix. It is in beta.

terms.network ownership: Which computer (the server or one player's device) is in charge of simulating a part's physics.
terms.assembly: A group of parts joined together that move as one object, like a car made of many parts welded together.
terms.unanchored: A part with `Anchored` set to false, so gravity and physics can move it.
terms.physics simulation: The math that decides how parts fall, bounce, roll, and collide each frame.
terms.WalkSpeed: A Humanoid property for how fast a character walks. The default is 16 studs per second, but a cheater can set their own to anything.
terms.Inf / NaN: Inf means infinity, a number too big to use. NaN means "not a number", a broken value. Both can mess up physics.
terms.fling: To launch a character or part away at a huge speed.
terms.latency: The delay for data to travel between the player and the server. It makes positions arrive a little late.
terms.heuristic: A rule of thumb used to guess something, like "moving more than 100 studs in 1 second is suspicious".
terms.leaky bucket: A counter that fills up when a player moves fast and slowly drains over time. Short bursts are fine, but staying too fast fills it and triggers a flag.
terms.XZ plane: The flat ground directions (X and Z), ignoring up and down (Y). Checking only XZ avoids punishing players who jump or fall.
terms.server authority: A new beta system where the server runs physics and movement, so players cannot fake them.

example.title: Keep an important ball owned by the server
example.place: Script in ServerScriptService (add an unanchored Part named GameBall to Workspace)
example.code:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

local ball = Workspace:WaitForChild("GameBall")

-- Passing nil makes the server own this part's physics,
-- so no player's device can control where it goes
if ball:CanSetNetworkOwnership() then
	ball:SetNetworkOwner(nil)
end
explain: The script finds the unanchored ball in Workspace.
`CanSetNetworkOwnership()` checks that ownership can be set for this part. It fails for anchored parts, for example.
`SetNetworkOwner(nil)` makes the server the owner, so a cheater near the ball cannot teleport or fling it.
The trade-off: the ball may look a bit less smooth to players because the server is doing the physics.

watchOut: Thinking players cannot change their own speed or position. They own their character, so the server must check anything important.
Making speed checks too strict. Players with laggy internet can look like they are teleporting; average over time.
Punishing jumping or falling. Check only ground movement on the XZ plane if your game is ground-based.
Forgetting your own teleports. If your game teleports players, tell your movement checker to allow it.
